claim: In Ko and Uttl (2003, N=75, Stata, 4 seeded bugs, 20 min) clustering gave three comprehension strategies (n=20/40/15) and none was clearly best: clusters 2 and 3 fixed more bugs than cluster 1 (1.65 and 2.00 vs 1.00, p<.05) but did not differ from each other. 'No strategy best' is a simplification; depth-first (c1) was worst overall.
agent_test: Run depth-first (one suspect until fixed) vs breadth-first (rank all suspects, probe each once) arms on the same debug items at equal tokens; compare bugs fixed per item.

claim: Strategy label tracked background (major, programming experience), not skill: cluster 2 had the least programming experience (1.20) yet beat cluster 1 (2.52). Strategy is partly a symptom of what the person already knows.
agent_test: Hold knowledge fixed (same retrieved notes in every arm) and check whether strategy arms still differ.

claim: Bug-specific knowledge and attitude were linked to fixing particular bugs (e.g. inverted axes: statistics test .40 vs .31, self-rated math 5.48 vs 4.41), while general vocabulary and problem-solving scores did not separate fixers. Evidence is per-bug univariate on N=75 with no multiple-test correction; the author's own thesis says experience, intelligence and statistics competence did not predict debugging success.
agent_test: Arm A: retrieve domain facts for the suspected bug class before search; arm B: no retrieval; same tokens. Score fix rate by bug class.

claim: Reading real output (graphs, results) before editing separated fixers in humans; the inverted-axes bug required graph inspection and was fixed by only 21% (16 of 75). Gap search 2026: no LLM study forces output inspection before the first edit; the nearest (SWT-Bench) uses self-written reproduction tests as a filter on finished patches (precision more than doubled for SWE-agent).
agent_test: Force an inspect-real-output step before the first edit vs allow edit first; compare fix rate on bugs that raise no error message.

claim: Surface cues steer attention whether or not they matter: a contradicting comment made one bug found by nearly twice as many as its twin, and fixing one often exposed the other. Observational, no manipulation. LLM side (CodeCrash, 17 LLMs, output prediction): misleading comments cut pass@1 about 24% on average; an 'ignore the comments' instruction did not fix it (GPT-4o direct 45.7 vs 45.9).
agent_test: Insert a misleading comment next to a true bug and next to a decoy in code items; measure whether the agent's first edit goes to the commented site, with and without a 'verify before trusting comments' guardrail.

claim: For LLMs, repair gains depend mainly on the accuracy of the diagnosis: GPT-4 repair 33.30% with its own feedback vs 52.60% with human feedback (16 participants, 40 programs); self-feedback was inaccurate in 32 of 80 cases vs 7 of 80 for humans; stronger-model feedback lifts weaker models. Counting total samples, self-repair gains are small.
agent_test: Same repair loop with self-critique vs independent critic vs critic given a retrieved lesson, equal total tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Without an external signal, LLM self-correction on reasoning does not help and often hurts (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0); with oracle labels the same loop gains (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3). Most harm is correct answers being changed.
agent_test: Revise-step on vs off with no new evidence; count correct-to-wrong flips at equal tokens. Allow a revision only when new tool or test evidence arrived.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Real execution output is the main driver of self-debugging gains: Self-Debug on TransCoder (Codex) 80.4 to 89.3 (simple) to 91.6 (unit tests); explanation alone helps mainly without tests; AutoSD with real debugger output gave 73% plausible patches vs 63% with model-imagined debugger output; LDB adds up to 9.8% with real intermediate values.
agent_test: Real tool output vs model-simulated output in the same debug loop; same token budget.
audit_note: Self-Debug 'Simple' feedback on TransCoder still uses unit-test pass/fail; table layout in the PDF is garbled but values 80.4/89.3/91.6 match.

claim: A human-derived debugging method (scientific debugging, rubber duck) adds little accuracy over plain LLM repair when no new information comes with it: AutoSD 76 vs 87 correct on Defects4J v1.2 and 113 vs 110 on v2.0; its value was explanations and a confidence signal.
agent_test: Hypothesis-prediction-experiment format vs free-form debugging, equal tokens, real execution available to both.

claim: Fixed locate-then-repair-then-validate pipelines match or beat free-strategy agents at lower cost on SWE-bench Lite (Agentless 32.00% at $0.70 vs SWE-agent GPT-4o 18.33% at $1.62), and resolve rate tracks correct localisation. Rivals: leaked or misleading issue text (4.3% exact patch, 5.0% misleading) and base-model strength. Update 2025-26: the fixed-route advantage faded with strong models. On the SWE-bench Verified leaderboard the best fixed multi-agent workflow (75.2%) is within 2 points of the best free single agent (73.2%); fixed no-agent pipelines are significantly lower; Agentless could not do multi-file edits on SWE-Bench Pro; its edge on SWE-PolyBench was Python-only.
agent_test: Fixed phases vs free action choice, same model and token cap, on a leak-filtered item set with confidence intervals.

claim: Information handed to the model dominates: same-model resolve rate more than doubles with oracle files (Claude 2: 1.96% BM25 vs 4.8% oracle), and six top agents solve largely the same issues (404 of 500 solved by at least one, 181 by all, 96 by none). New: SWE-Bench Pro, adding requirements and interface text raised GPT-5 from 8.4% to 25.9% and Opus 4.1 from 8.2% to 22.7%; file naming from issue text alone reaches 76% on Verified vs under 53% on outside repositories.
agent_test: Give correct-file context vs retrieved context vs none; measure fix rate at equal tokens.
audit_note: SWE-Bench Pro notes the problem-only setting suffers false negatives from unit-test verifiers, so part of the 8.4-to-25.9 jump is under-specification; numbers match.

claim: Interface and tool output format change results with the model fixed: SWE-agent GPT-4 Turbo 18.0% default vs 10.3% without the edit command; iterative search 12.0% vs no search 15.7%; 100-line viewer 18.0% vs whole file 12.7%. After one failed edit, chance of eventual success drops from 90.5% to 57.2%.
agent_test: Cap tool-output size and require re-localise after a failed edit vs no cap; equal tokens.

claim: Runtime feedback is not uniformly useful: it helps syntax and reference bugs and does not help or can hurt logic bugs; debugging success varies strongly with bug class.
agent_test: Route by suspected bug class: raw trace feedback only for syntax or reference, value-level probes for logic; compare to uniform trace feedback.

claim: Depth-first fixation on one suspect costs coverage in both humans (Ko and Uttl cluster 1: 1.00 bugs) and agents (SWE-agent iterative search worse than none: 12.0 vs 15.7). Different mechanisms, similar shape; not a controlled link. New: failed agent runs show repeated identical actions and fixes without testing (Bouzenia and Pradel, 120 trajectories); structured backtracking lifted five models on SWE-bench Lite by +23% relative but at higher call cost.
agent_test: Cap effort per hypothesis and force a round-robin over the top suspects vs unlimited depth; equal tokens.

claim: Hard real bugs need information gathering before editing: in live-streamed work, long episodes had first edit at 3.2 min vs 6 s for short ones; half of reported-defect episodes ended unfixed. A fast first edit marks an easy bug.
agent_test: Compare minimum probing steps before first edit; do not reward speed to first edit in scoring.

claim: Beller et al. (176 developers surveyed, 723 IDE sessions) found no correlation between developer experience and use of an IDE debugger or unit tests for debugging, with printf debugging common; Ko and Uttl (2003, lab study) found that three comprehension strategies were related to programming experience but no strategy gave better debugging performance (domain knowledge of the bug and computer attitudes predicted success). Both suggest strategy choice is not the main driver of debugging success, but they differ on whether strategy tracks experience. Neither manipulated strategy experimentally.
agent_test: Do not copy 'expert strategy' as a prior; test candidate strategies as arms.
audit_note: Beller et al. found no correlation between experience and use of an IDE debugger or tests, but Ko and Uttl found comprehension strategies WERE related to programming experience (and not to success), so the two do not agree on experience; the b28 synthesis is the same Beller PDF listed twice.
claim_before_audit: Real developers' strategy choice (printf vs debugger) does not map onto experience (no correlation, 176 surveyed, 723 sessions), agreeing with Ko and Uttl that strategy is habit and background more than skill. Neither study measures strategy-outcome in a manipulated design.

claim: Failures cluster in wrong diagnosis and weak verification rather than strategy: 52.0% of unresolved SWE-agent runs were wrong or over-specific implementations; unresolved runs ran longer (21 vs 12 steps); multi-agent failures 21.3% task-verification category. Grounded confidence signals help only if tied to real execution (<DONE> 89% vs 82%).
agent_test: Stop-and-rediagnose trigger after N failed attempts vs continue; measure resolve rate at equal tokens.
audit_note: 21 steps is a mean for unresolved vs 12 a median for resolved; 'rather than strategy' is the notes' interpretation, not tested in the papers.

claim: Forward-citation check done: 56 papers cite Ko and Uttl (2003) in Semantic Scholar and none is a replication; none is an LLM study testing strategy against knowledge. Nearest LLM work: Bouzenia and Pradel (2025) compare action patterns of 120 agent trajectories by success; SWE-Bench Pro clusters failure modes with an LLM judge. No study crosses strategy with information at equal tokens. The stronger human claim remains single-source.
agent_test: 2x2 on our items: (fixed vs free strategy) x (execution feedback or retrieved knowledge on vs off); read the interaction.

claim: Boundary: the finding comes from an unfamiliar language, novices, seeded bugs, 20 minutes; the authors hypothesise strategy matters more once the system is familiar. The Ko thesis found strategy predicted success when writing new code but not when debugging. New 2025-26 evidence is indirect: models do worse in less common languages (SWE-PolyBench Python 20-24% vs TypeScript 5-13%), retrieval helps most for rare libraries (CodeRAG-Bench ODEX-hard), and in a rare DSL the model matters more than the harness (BC-Bench). No study shows the strategy effect growing with familiarity.
agent_test: Run the strategy arms on familiar-language vs rare-language items and see whether the strategy effect grows with familiarity.

claim: A retrieved distilled lesson from past issues lifts resolve rate a few points with the model fixed, but more than one lesson or a forced citation of it hurts. SWE-Exp, Verified, DeepSeek-V3: 0 lessons 37.8%, 1 lesson 42.0%, 2 lessons 39.8%, 4 lessons 39.0%; no abstraction (raw demos) 36.0%. Deliberately false facts were not tested.
agent_test: Bug-class lesson store: 0, 1, 2 lessons, and one wrong lesson, on the same items and token cap; measure fix rate and how often the wrong lesson is followed.

claim: Misleading comments steer LLMs (CodeCrash: about 24% average relative drop in output prediction for 17 LLMs; reasoning models spend 2-3 times more tokens on plausible wrong hints), and a verbal guardrail 'ignore the comments' did not remove the effect under direct inference (GPT-4o 45.7 vs 45.9). A refactor-first pass made it worse (45.7 to 41.1). Chain of thought recovers part (DeepSeek-V3 70.2 to 82.1).
agent_test: Guardrail as an action (run or check before trusting a comment) vs a guardrail as a sentence; compare with no guardrail on misleading-comment items.

claim: Knowledge of the specific repository matters for LLMs in the way bug-specific knowledge mattered for humans: issue text alone names the buggy file up to 76% of the time on SWE-Bench Verified and under 53% on outside repositories; benchmark strategy comparisons on Verified are confounded by this.
agent_test: Run strategy arms on leak-filtered or post-cutoff items and on rare-library items; compare the strategy effect to the same arms on Verified.

claim: With strong 2025 models a fixed workflow no longer clearly beats a free single agent: Verified leaderboard 75.2% (fixed multi-agent) vs 73.2% (autonomous single agent); fixed no-agent pipelines significantly lower (Dunn p=0.0207, 0.0125, 0.0003 vs three groups). On Lite no group difference (p=0.0579).
agent_test: Same strong model, fixed locate-fix-validate vs free choice, on Verified-like and multi-file items at equal tokens.

claim: No published 2x2 (fixed vs free strategy by information on or off, equal tokens, one model) was found for 2024-2026. Closest are scaffold-by-model (SWE-Effi: SWE-Agent 28% with Qwen3-32B vs 10% with GPT-4o-mini; AutoCodeRover 38% with 14.7 calls), model-vs-harness in a rare DSL (BC-Bench: model p=0.026 and 0.019, harness p=0.728 and 0.075) and information on/off (SWE-Bench Pro 25.9 vs 8.4).
agent_test: Run the 2x2 ourselves: this is the decisive experiment for the whole subfield.

claim: Stop-and-rediagnose evidence is thin. Structured backtracking (SWE-Search) gave +23% relative on Lite at higher call cost; free state transitions alone gave only +1.4%; stuck runs burn far more tokens (SWE-Effi 'expensive failures'); failed SWE-agent runs show repeated identical actions. No equal-token test of a failure-count trigger exists.
agent_test: Trigger a re-diagnosis after k failed edits (k=2,3) vs continue; equal tokens; report fix rate and token use on failed items.
